title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 890–892 (Night 214, continuing nights-213), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 214 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Under the trapdoor he finds a stair down to an ancient rock-cut hall from the days of ʿĀd and Thamūd, full of red gold. The gardener brings news that the merchants' ship sails in three days for the Ebony Isle, the first stage of the road home; Qamar al-Zamān tells him of the treasure, and they share it, twenty jars of gold, half each. On the gardener's advice he packs his share in fifty jars under a layer of olives, hides the stone in one of them, and waits, longing for Budūr. Then the old gardener falls ill; while Qamar al-Zamān sits at his deathbed the sailors carry the jars aboard and urge him to hurry, and by the time he has closed the old man's eyes and buried him the ship has sailed. He is left in the orchard, throwing dust on his head; and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الرَّابِعَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-rābiʿata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fourteenth after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and fourteenth night,
sentences.n: al-rābiʿata ʿashara, “fourteenth”: as in the nights before, the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا فَتَحَ ذٰلِكَ الطَّابَقَ وَجَدَ بَابًا وَسُلَّمًا فَنَزَلَ فِيهِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā fataḥa dhālika al-ṭābaqa wajada bāban wa-sullaman fa-nazala fīhi
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that Qamar al-Zamān, when he-opened that trapdoor, found a-door and-a-ladder, and-he-went-down in-it.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Qamar al-Zamān opened that trapdoor he found a door and a flight of steps, and went down into it.
sentences.n: Qamara is accusative after anna. lammā … wajada, “when he opened … he found”: lammā with a perfect sets the time of the main verb. al-ṭābaq is the trapdoor he uncovered under the carob tree at the end of the night before. sullam, “ladder, stair”; the ḍamma and the shadda of وسُلّما are printed. nazala fī, “to go down into”: fī marks where, and -hi points back to the opening.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ قَاعَةً قَدِيمَةً مِنْ عَهْدِ عَادٍ وَثَمُودَ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada qāʿatan qadīmatan min ʿahdi ʿĀdin wa-Thamūda
sentences.l: And-he-found a-hall ancient from (the) time (of) ʿĀd and-Thamūd.
sentences.i: There he found an ancient hall, from the days of ʿĀd and Thamūd.
sentences.n: ʿĀd and Thamūd are the two vanished peoples of old Arabia whom the Qurʾān names; “from the time of ʿĀd and Thamūd” is a stock way of saying “immeasurably old”. ʿahd, “time, era”. Thamūd is a diptote, so its genitive ends in -a without tanwīn; the short name ʿĀd takes tanwīn.

sentences.t: وَهٰذِهِ الْقَاعَةُ مَنْقُورَةٌ مِنَ الْحَجَرِ وَاهًا دَوَائِرُ سَمَاوِيَّاتٌ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi al-qāʿatu manqūratun mina al-ḥajari wāhan dawāʾiru samāwiyyātun
sentences.l: And-this the-hall (was) hollowed-out from the-rock — ah-how-fine! — circles heavenly.
sentences.i: This hall was hewn out of the rock: ah, what heavenly circles!
sentences.n: The print has وهذة, a misprint for وهذه, corrected here. manqūra, “hollowed, carved out”, passive participle of naqara, “to peck, carve”: min al-ḥajari, “out of the rock”, min marks the stuff it is cut from. The next word is doubtful. The print has واها, which as its letters stand can only be the exclamation wāhan, “ah, how fine!”, and it is vocalised and translated so here: the narrator breaks off to admire the hall, and dawāʾiru samāwiyyātun, “heavenly circles”, stands on its own. The sentence would run more smoothly if the word were a slip for ولها, wa-lahā, “and it has (heavenly circles)”; that is likely but not certain, so the print is kept. dawāʾir, plural of dāʾira, “circle”: perhaps carved or painted figures of the heavenly spheres, perhaps round vaults like the sky; its ئ is printed, and as a diptote it has -u without tanwīn. samāwiyyāt, “heavenly”, a feminine sound plural agreeing with the broken plural dawāʾir.

sentences.t: وَوَجَدَهَا مَمْلُوءَةً مِنَ الذَّهَبِ الْأَحْمَرِ الْوَهَّاجِ فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ لَقَدْ ذَهَبَ التَّعَبُ وَجَاءَ الْفَرَجُ وَالسُّرُورُ
sentences.tr: wa-wajadahā mamlūʾatan mina al-dhahabi al-aḥmari al-wahhāji fa-qāla fī nafsihi la-qad dhahaba al-taʿabu wa-jāʾa al-faraju wa-al-surūru
sentences.l: And-he-found-it filled with the-gold the-red the-blazing; and-he-said in his-soul: Indeed already has-gone the-toil, and-has-come the-relief and-the-joy.
sentences.i: And he found it full of red gold, blazing bright; and he said to himself, “Now the toil is over, and relief and joy have come.”
sentences.n: wajadahā mamlūʾatan, “he found it filled”: the accusative participle tells the state he found it in. mamlūʾ is the passive participle of malaʾa, “to fill”, and its hamza is printed; min marks what fills it. al-dhahab al-aḥmar, “red gold”, the stock phrase for pure gold; wahhāj, “blazing, glowing”. qāla fī nafsihi, “he said in his soul”, that is, to himself. la-qad, “now truly”: la- strengthens qad with the perfect. Mark the play of dhahab, “gold”, and dhahaba, “has gone”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ طَلَعَ مِنَ الْمَكَانِ إِلَى ظَاهِرِ الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni ṭalaʿa mina al-makāni ilā ẓāhiri al-bustāni
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān came-up from the-place to (the) outside (of) the-garden,
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān climbed out of the place up to the open ground of the garden,
sentences.n: thumma inna, the narrator's “then”: Qamara is accusative after inna. ṭalaʿa min … ilā, “to come up from … to”. ẓāhir, “outside, surface”: ẓāhir al-bustān is the garden above ground, as against the hall beneath it. The rhyme of al-makān / al-bustān is the storyteller's sajʿ.

sentences.t: وَرَدَّ الطَّابَقَ كَمَا كَانَ وَرَجَعَ إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ وَحَوَّلَ الْمَاءَ عَلَى الْأَشْجَارِ إِلَى آخِرِ النَّهَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-radda al-ṭābaqa kamā kāna wa-rajaʿa ilā al-bustāni wa-ḥawwala al-māʾa ʿalā al-ashjāri ilā ākhiri al-nahāri
sentences.l: and-he-put-back the-trapdoor as it-was, and-returned to the-garden, and-turned the-water onto the-trees till (the) end (of) the-day.
sentences.i: and put the trapdoor back as it had been, and went back to the garden and turned the water on to the trees until the end of the day.
sentences.n: radda, “to give back, put back”; its shadda is printed. kamā kāna, “as it was”. rajaʿa ilā al-bustān, “he went back to the garden”, that is, to his work in it. ḥawwala, Form II, “to turn, divert”, here the channels that water the orchard: ʿalā marks the trees the water is led onto; its shadda is printed. ilā ākhiri al-nahāri, “until the end of the day”: ilā marks the limit of time, and the madda of آخر is printed. The rhyme falls on al-ashjār / al-nahār.

sentences.t: فَجَاءَ الْخَوْلِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي أَبْشِرْ بِرُجُوعِكَ إِلَى الْأَوْطَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-jāʾa al-khawliyyu wa-qāla lahu yā waladī abshir bi-rujūʿika ilā al-awṭāni
sentences.l: And-came the-gardener and-said to-him: O my-son, rejoice in-your-returning to the-homelands,
sentences.i: Then the gardener came and said to him, “My son, good news: you are going back to your homeland,
sentences.n: abshir, Form IV imperative, “rejoice, take the good news”: bi- marks what the good news is. rujūʿ, “return”, a verbal noun with the suffix as its subject: “your returning”. al-awṭān, plural of waṭan, “homeland”; the plural is the usual way of speaking of one's home country.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّ التُّجَّارَ تَجَهَّزُوا لِلسَّفَرِ وَالْمَرْكَبُ بَعْدَ ثَلٰثَةِ أَيَّامٍ مُسَافِرَةٌ إِلَى مَدِينَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ وَهِيَ أَوَّلُ مَدِينَةٍ مِنْ مَدَائِنِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-inna al-tujjāra tajahhazū li-al-safari wa-al-markabu baʿda thalāthati ayyāmin musāfiratun ilā madīnati al-ābanūsi wa-hiya awwalu madīnatin min madāʾini al-muslimīna
sentences.l: for indeed the-merchants have-made-ready for-the-journey, and-the-ship after three days (is) setting-out to (the) city (of) the-ebony; and-it (is the) first city of (the) cities (of) the-Muslims.
sentences.i: for the merchants have made ready for the voyage, and in three days the ship sails for the City of Ebony, which is the first of the cities of the Muslims.
sentences.n: tajahhaza li-, Form V, “to get oneself ready for”: li- marks what one readies for; the shadda of تجهّزوا is printed. wa-al-markabu … musāfiratun, “and the ship (is) setting out”: the participle is feminine, though markab is masculine; the print treats the ship as feminine here and again at the night's end, as the spoken language often does. ثلثة is the print's spelling of thalātha, “three”, pointed with a dagger alif. ābanūs is “ebony”, and the madda of الآبنوس is printed; the place is called a city here and an island a little later. madāʾin, plural of madīna, “city”; its ئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَإِذَا وَصَلْتَ إِلَيْهَا تُسَافِرُ فِى الْبَرِّ سِتَّةَ أَشْهُرٍ حَتَّى تَصِلَ إِلَى جَزَائِرِ خَالِدَانَ الَّتِي فِيهَا الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-idhā waṣalta ilayhā tusāfiru fī al-barri sittata ashhurin ḥattā taṣila ilā jazāʾiri Khālidāna allatī fīhā al-maliku Shahramānu
sentences.l: And-when you-arrive to-it, you-travel in the-land six months until you-reach to (the) islands (of) Khālidān, which in-them (is) the-king Shahramān.
sentences.i: When you reach it, you travel overland for six months until you come to the Islands of Khālidān, where King Shahramān is.”
sentences.n: idhā … tusāfiru, “when … you travel”: the answer to idhā is a plain imperfect, which needs no fa-. fī al-barri, “by land”, as against by sea; the shadda of البرّ is printed, and فى is spelt with ى. sittata ashhurin, “six months”, an accusative of time. ḥattā taṣila, “until you reach”: subjunctive after ḥattā. The ئ of جزائر is printed; Khālidān, a diptote, has -a in the genitive. allatī fīhā, “in which (is)”: -hā points back to the islands. King Shahramān is Qamar al-Zamān's father, so the gardener is telling him the road home.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ بِذٰلِكَ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa bi-dhālika wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And-he-rejoiced in-that, and-recited, saying:
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān rejoiced at this, and recited:
sentences.n: fariḥa bi-, “to rejoice at”: bi- marks the cause of the joy. anshada yaqūlu, “he recited, saying”, the formula that brings in verse.

sentences.t:
لَاتَهْجُرُوْا مَنْ لَا تَعَوَّدَ هَجْرَكُمْ * وَتُعَذِّبُوْا بِصُدُوْدِكُمْ مَنْ لَاجَنَا
غَيْرِي اِذَا طَالَ الْبِعَادُ سَلَاكُمُ * وَتَغَيَّرَتْ اَحْوَالُهُ اِلَّا اَنَا
sentences.tr:
lā tahjurū man lā taʿawwada hajrakum * wa-tuʿadhdhibū bi-ṣudūdikum man lā janā
ghayrī idhā ṭāla al-biʿādu salākumu * wa-taghayyarat aḥwāluhu illā anā
sentences.l:
Do-not forsake one-who not grew-used-to your-forsaking, * and-torment with-your-turning-away one-who not did-wrong;
other-than-me, when grows-long the-distance, forgets-you, * and-change his-states — except I.
sentences.i:
Do not forsake one who never learned to bear your forsaking, * nor torment with your coldness one who has done no wrong.
Another, when the parting grows long, forgets you, * and his heart is changed; but not I.
sentences.n: The print has وَتُعَلِّبُوْا, a misprint for وتعذبوا, corrected here and vocalised wa-tuʿadhdhibū; the rest of the verse is copied as printed. The lā of the prohibition carries over: wa-tuʿadhdhibū, “and (do not) torment”. The print sets lā tahjurū solid as لَاتَهْجُرُوْا, and lā janā as لَاجَنَا. taʿawwada, Form V, “to grow used to”. bi-ṣudūdikum: bi- marks the means, ṣudūd, “turning away, coldness”. janā, “to commit an offence”, here without an object. salā, “to be consoled for, forget”, here with a direct object: salākumu, “forgets you”, with the long -u on the pronoun that the metre wants. aḥwāl, plural of ḥāl, “state, condition”. The rhyme falls on janā / anā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ قَبَّلَ يَدَ الْخَوْلِيِّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَالِدِي كَمَا أَنَّكَ بَشَّرْتَنِي فَأَنَا الْآخَرُ أُبَشِّرُكَ بِشَارَةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni qabbala yada al-khawliyyi wa-qāla lahu yā wālidī kamā annaka bashshartanī fa-anā al-ākharu ubashshiruka bishāratan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān kissed (the) hand (of) the-gardener and-said to-him: O my-father, just as you brought-me-good-news, so-I, the-other, bring-you-good-news, a-tidings great.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān kissed the gardener's hand and said to him, “Father, as you have brought me good news, so I in my turn bring you great good news.”
sentences.n: qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”; its shadda is printed, as are those of بشّرتني and ابشّرك. yā wālidī, “O my father”, a young man's courtesy to an old one, answering the old man's yā waladī, “my son”. kamā annaka … fa-anā, “just as you … so I”: fa- brings in the matching half. anā al-ākharu, “I, the other”, that is, “I too, in my turn”; its madda is printed. bashshara, Form II, “to bring (someone) good news”; bishāra, “good tidings”, stands as its object.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَخْبَرَهُ بِخَبَرِ الْقَاعَةِ الَّتِي رَآهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahu akhbarahu bi-khabari al-qāʿati allatī raʾāhā
sentences.l: Then indeed-he informed-him of-(the)-news (of) the-hall which he-had-seen-it.
sentences.i: And he told him about the hall he had seen.
sentences.n: akhbara … bi-, Form IV, “to tell (someone) of”: bi- marks what is told; khabar, “news, account”, is from the same root. allatī raʾāhā, “which he saw (it)”: -hā points back to the hall. The madda of رآها is printed.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ الْخَوْلِيُّ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي إِنِّي فِي هٰذَا الْبُسْتَانِ مِنْ ثَمَانِينَ عَامًا مَا وَقَفْتُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa al-khawliyyu wa-qāla lahu yā waladī innī fī hādhā al-bustāni min thamānīna ʿāman mā waqaftu ʿalā shayʾin
sentences.l: And-rejoiced the-gardener and-said to-him: O my-son, indeed-I (am) in this garden from eighty years; not I-came-upon anything,
sentences.i: The gardener rejoiced and said to him, “My son, I have been in this garden these eighty years and have never come upon a thing,
sentences.n: innī fī hādhā al-bustāni min thamānīna ʿāman, “I am in this garden since eighty years”: min marks the time from which, where English says “for”. thamānīn, “eighty”, takes the singular accusative ʿāman, “year”. waqafa ʿalā, “to stand upon”, and so “to come upon, find”: ʿalā marks what is found. The hamza of شيء is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَنْتَ لَكَ عِنْدِي دُونَ السَّنَةِ وَقَدْ رَأَيْتَ هٰذَا الْأَمْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-anta laka ʿindī dūna al-sanati wa-qad raʾayta hādhā al-amra
sentences.l: and-you, for-you with-me (is) under the-year, and-already you-have-seen this the-thing.
sentences.i: and you have been with me less than a year, and you have come upon this.
sentences.n: wa-anta laka ʿindī dūna al-sanati, “and you, there is to you with me under the year”: a homely way of counting time spent with someone, li- marking whose time it is; dūna, “below, short of”. raʾā here is “to come to see, find”; the hamza of رأيت is printed.

sentences.t: فَهُوَ رِزْقُكَ وَسَبَبُ زَوَالِ عَكْسِكَ وَمُعِينٌ لَكَ عَلَى وُصُولِكَ إِلَى أَهْلِكَ وَجَمْعِ شَمْلِكَ بِمَنْ تُحِبُّ
sentences.tr: fa-huwa rizquka wa-sababu zawāli ʿaksika wa-muʿīnun laka ʿalā wuṣūlika ilā ahlika wa-jamʿi shamlika bi-man tuḥibbu
sentences.l: So-it (is) your-portion, and-(the)-cause (of the) passing (of) your-reverse, and-a-helper for-you towards your-arriving to your-people and-(the)-gathering (of) your-scattered-state with-whom you-love.
sentences.i: It is your appointed portion, and the end of your ill fortune, and a help to bring you home to your people and reunite you with the one you love.”
sentences.n: rizq, “provision, livelihood”, what God allots to each. ʿaks, “reversal, ill luck”, a word of the later language: zawāl ʿaksika, “the passing of your bad luck”. muʿīn ʿalā, “a helper towards”: ʿalā marks what is helped towards, and li- in laka the one helped. jamʿ al-shaml, “gathering what was scattered”, the stock phrase for reunion: bi- marks the one he is reunited with. The shadda of تحبّ is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ لَا بُدَّ مِنَ الْقِسْمَةِ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni lā budda mina al-qismati baynī wa-baynaka
sentences.l: And-said Qamar al-Zamān: (There is) no escape from the-dividing between-me and-between-you.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said, “It must be shared between us.”
sentences.n: lā budda min, “there is no escape from”, that is, “it must be”: min marks what cannot be avoided. qisma, “dividing, sharing”. Arabic repeats bayna with each pronoun: baynī wa-baynaka, “between me and you”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذَ الْخَوْلِيَّ وَدَخَلَ بِهِ إِلَى ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَأَرَاهُ الذَّهَبَ وَكَانَ فِي عِشْرِينَ خَابِيَةً فَأَخَذَ عَشَرَةً وَالْخَوْلِيُّ عَشَرَةً
sentences.tr: thumma akhadha al-khawliyya wa-dakhala bihi ilā dhālika al-makāni wa-arāhu al-dhahaba wa-kāna fī ʿishrīna khābiyatan fa-akhadha ʿasharatan wa-al-khawliyyu ʿasharatan
sentences.l: Then he-took the-gardener and-went-in with-him to that place and-showed-him the-gold; and-it-was in twenty jars; and-he-took ten, and-the-gardener ten.
sentences.i: Then he took the gardener down into that place and showed him the gold, which lay in twenty great jars; and he took ten, and the gardener ten.
sentences.n: The print has واراة, a misprint for واراه, corrected here. dakhala bi-, “to go in with, take in”: bi- marks the one brought along. arāhu, Form IV of raʾā, “he showed him”, takes two objects, the man and the gold. khābiya, “large earthenware jar”, the kind set in the ground to store oil or grain; ʿishrīn takes the singular accusative. ʿasharatan, “ten”, is the form with -a(t), the one used in counting and in the spoken language, though for the feminine khābiya Classical Arabic would say ʿashran. wa-al-khawliyyu ʿasharatan, “and the gardener (took) ten”: the verb is understood from the clause before.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَوْلِيُّ يَا وَلَدِي عَبِّ لَكَ أَمْطَارًا مِنَ الزَّيْتُونِ الْعَصَافِيرِيِّ الَّذِي فِي هٰذَا الْبُسْتَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khawliyyu yā waladī ʿabbi laka amṭāran mina al-zaytūni al-ʿaṣāfīriyyi alladhī fī hādhā al-bustāni
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-gardener: O my-son, pack for-yourself jars of the-olives the-ʿaṣāfīrī which (is) in this garden,
sentences.i: Then the gardener said to him, “My son, fill yourself some jars with the ʿaṣāfīrī olives that grow in this garden,
sentences.n: ʿabbi, imperative of ʿabbā, Form II, “to fill, pack (a vessel)”, a word of the later language; its kasra and shadda are printed. laka, “for yourself”: li- marks whom the work is for. amṭār, plural of maṭar, is not “rain” here but a large jar for oil and olives, a sense recorded for the later language (Dozy). al-zaytūn al-ʿaṣāfīrī is a kind of olive; the name looks like a relative adjective from ʿaṣāfīr, “sparrows”, perhaps for a small fruit, but the variety cannot be pinned down.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهُ مَعْدُومٌ فِي غَيْرِ بِلَادِنَا وَتَجْلِبُهُ التُّجَّارُ إِلَى جَمِيعِ الْبُلْدَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-innahu maʿdūmun fī ghayri bilādinā wa-tajlibuhu al-tujjāru ilā jamīʿi al-buldāni
sentences.l: for indeed-it (is) not-to-be-had in other-than our-lands, and-bring-it the-merchants to all the-countries;
sentences.i: for it is not to be found outside our country, and the merchants carry it to every land.
sentences.n: maʿdūm, “lacking, not to be had”, passive participle of ʿadima. tajlibuhu al-tujjāru: a feminine verb with the broken plural tujjār, “merchants”, as is allowed. jalaba … ilā, “to bring (goods) to”: ilā marks where. bilād and buldān, “lands, countries”, are two plurals of one word, set at either end of the sentence.

sentences.t: وَاخْلِطْهُ مَعَ الذَّهَبِ وَلَبِّسْهُمْ وَاجْعَلِ الذَّهَبَ فِى الْأَمْطَارِ وَالزَّيْتَ فَوْقَ الذَّهَبِ ثُمَّ سُدَّهَا وَخُذْهَا مَعَكَ فِى الْمَرْكَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-ikhliṭhu maʿa al-dhahabi wa-labbishum wa-ijʿali al-dhahaba fī al-amṭāri wa-al-zayta fawqa al-dhahabi thumma suddahā wa-khudhhā maʿaka fī al-markabi
sentences.l: and-mix-it with the-gold, and-cover-them-over: and-put the-gold in the-jars and-the-oil above the-gold; then stop-them-up and-take-them with-you in the-ship.
sentences.i: and mix them with the gold and cover them over: put the gold in the jars and the oil on top of the gold, then stop them up and take them with you on the ship.”
sentences.n: ikhliṭhu, “mix it”: -hu points to the olives. labbis, Form II imperative of a verb meaning “to clothe, cover”, here “to cover over, hide” the gold beneath the olives; its shadda is printed. -hum, “them”, is a masculine plural suffix for the jars, as the spoken language uses it of things. al-zayt, “oil”: the olives go in with their oil, so that the gold lies hidden at the bottom. sadda, “to stop up, seal”: suddahā, “seal them”, -hā for the jars; its shadda is printed. Both فى are spelt with ى.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مِنْ وَقْتِهِ وَسَاعَتِهِ وَعَبَّى خَمْسِينَ مَطَرًا وَوَضَعَ الذَّهَبَ فِيهَا وَسَدَّ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma Qamaru al-Zamāni min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi wa-ʿabbā khamsīna maṭaran wa-waḍaʿa al-dhahaba fīhā wa-sadda ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-rose Qamar al-Zamān from his-time and-his-hour, and-packed fifty jars, and-put the-gold in-them, and-shut (them) over-it,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān rose that very hour and filled fifty jars; he put the gold in them and sealed it in,
sentences.n: min waqtihi wa-sāʿatihi, “from his time and his hour”, a stock phrase for “at once”. ʿabbā, Form II, “to fill, pack”; its shadda is printed. maṭar, “jar”, singular accusative after khamsīn, “fifty”. sadda ʿalā, “to shut in, seal over”: ʿalā marks what is shut in, the gold; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَبَّسَ عَلَيْهِمْ بَعْدَ أَنْ جَعَلَ الزَّيْتُونَ فَوْقَ الذَّهَبِ وَحَطَّ الْفَصَّ مَعَهُ فِي مَطَرٍ
sentences.tr: wa-labbasa ʿalayhim baʿda an jaʿala al-zaytūna fawqa al-dhahabi wa-ḥaṭṭa al-faṣṣa maʿahu fī maṭarin
sentences.l: and-covered-over upon-them, after that he-put the-olives above the-gold; and-he-set the-stone with-it in a-jar.
sentences.i: and covered it over, having laid the olives on top of the gold; and he put the gem in one of the jars along with it.
sentences.n: labbasa ʿalā, Form II, “to cover over, disguise”: ʿalā marks what is hidden; as in the gardener's words, the gold is masked by the olives, and -him is again the jars; its shadda is printed. But labbasa ʿalā is also “to make a thing obscure to someone, deceive”, so ʿalayhim may be people, “and he disguised it from them”; either way the gold is hidden. baʿda an jaʿala, “after he had put”. ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, set”, a word much used in the later language; its shadda is printed. al-faṣṣ, “the stone, the gem”: the one he found in the bird's crop in the night before, the cause of his parting from his wife. maʿahu, “with it”, with the gold. fī maṭarin, “in a jar”, one of the fifty.

sentences.t: وَجَلَسَ هُوَ وَالْخَوْلِيُّ يَتَحَدَّثَانِ وَأَيْقَنَ بِجَمْعِ شَمْلِهِ وَقُرْبِهِ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-jalasa huwa wa-al-khawliyyu yataḥaddathāni wa-ayqana bi-jamʿi shamlihi wa-qurbihi min ahlihi
sentences.l: And-sat he and-the-gardener, (the two) talking-together; and-he-was-certain of-(the)-gathering (of) his-scattered-state and-his-nearness to his-people.
sentences.i: Then he and the gardener sat talking together; and he was sure now of being reunited with his own and of drawing near to his people.
sentences.n: jalasa huwa wa-al-khawliyyu, “he sat, he and the gardener”: the verb comes first and stays singular; huwa is spelt out so that the gardener can be joined to the subject. yataḥaddathāni, dual imperfect, “the two of them talking”, tells how they sat; taḥaddatha, Form V, “to talk together”, has its shadda printed. ayqana bi-, Form IV, “to be certain of”: the verb takes bi- for what one is sure of. qurb min, “nearness to”: min marks what one is near.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ إِذَا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى جَزِيرَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ أُسَافِرُ مِنْهَا إِلَى بِلَادِ أَبِي وَأَسْأَلُ عَنْ مَحْبُوبَتِي بُدُورَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla fī nafsihi idhā waṣaltu ilā jazīrati al-ābanūsi usāfiru minhā ilā bilādi abī wa-asʾalu ʿan maḥbūbatī Budūra
sentences.l: And-he-said in his-soul: When I-arrive to (the) island (of) the-ebony, I-travel from-it to (the) lands (of) my-father, and-ask about my-beloved Budūr.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “When I reach the Isle of Ebony, I will travel on from there to my father's country and ask after my beloved Budūr.
sentences.n: jazīrat al-ābanūs, “the Isle of Ebony”: the gardener called it a city, madīna, and it is both; the madda of الآبنوس is printed. idhā … usāfiru, “when … I travel”, again with no fa- before the answer. saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿan marks what is asked after; the hamza of واسأل is printed. Budūr, a diptote, has -a in the genitive, in apposition to maḥbūbatī.

sentences.t: فَيَاتُرَى هَلْ رَجَعَتْ إِلَى بِلَادِهَا أَوْ سَافَرَتْ إِلَى بِلَادِ أَبِي أَوْحَدَثَ لَهَا حَادِثٌ فِى الطَّرِيقِ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-yā turā hal rajaʿat ilā bilādihā aw sāfarat ilā bilādi abī aw ḥadatha lahā ḥādithun fī al-ṭarīqi thumma anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: So-O-is-it-seen: did she-return to her-lands, or she-travelled to (the) lands (of) my-father, or happened to-her a-happening on the-road? Then he-recited, saying:
sentences.i: I wonder: did she go back to her own country, or travel on to my father's, or did some mishap befall her on the way?” Then he recited:
sentences.n: fa-yā turā, “I wonder”, literally “O, is it seen?”, a colloquial opener for a question; the print sets it solid as فياترى. It also sets aw ḥadatha, “or happened”, solid as اوحدث; both are kept as printed. ḥadatha lahā ḥādithun, “a happening happened to her”, a mishap: li- marks the one it befalls, and ḥādith comes from the same root as the verb. فى is spelt with ى. anshada yaqūlu brings in the verse.

sentences.t:
اَقَامُوا الْوَجْدَ فِيْ قَلْبِيْ وَسَارُوْا * وَقَدْ شَطَّتْ بِمَنْ اَهْوَى الدِّيَارُ
نَأَتْ عَنِّي الرَّبُوْعُ وَسَاكِنِيْهَا * وَقَدْ بَعُدَ الْمَزَارُ فَلَا مَزَارُ
وَبَانَ تَجَلُّديْ مِنْ حَيْثُ بَانُوا * وَفَارَقَنِيْ هُجُوْعٌ وَاصْطِبَارُ
وَمُذْ سَارُوْا سَرَىٰ عَنِّيْ سُرُوْرِيْ * وَقَدْ عُدِمَ الْقَرَارُ فَلَا قَرَارُ
وَاَجْرَوْا بِالْفِرَاقِ دُمُوْعَ عَيَنِيْ * فَاَدْمَعُهَا بِبَيْنِهِمُ غِزَارُ
اِذَا مَا اشْتَقْتُ يَوْمًا اَنْ اَرَاهَمْ * وَزَادَ بِهِمْ حَنِيْنِيْ وَاِنْتِظَارُ
اُمَثِّلُ شَخْصَهُمْ فِيْ وَسْطِ قَلْبِيْ * غَرَامٌ وَاشْتِيَاقٌ وَادِّكَارُ
sentences.tr:
aqāmū al-wajda fī qalbī wa-sārū * wa-qad shaṭṭat bi-man ahwā al-diyāru
naʾat ʿannī al-rabūʿu wa-sākinīhā * wa-qad baʿuda al-mazāru fa-lā mazāru
wa-bāna tajalludī min ḥaythu bānū * wa-fāraqanī hujūʿun wa-iṣṭibāru
wa-mudh sārū sarā ʿannī surūrī * wa-qad ʿudima al-qarāru fa-lā qarāru
wa-ajraw bi-al-firāqi dumūʿa ʿayanī * fa-admaʿuhā bi-baynihimu ghizāru
idhā mā ishtaqtu yawman an arāham * wa-zāda bihim ḥanīnī wa-intiẓāru
umaththilu shakhṣahum fī wasṭi qalbī * gharāmun wa-ishtiyāqun wa-iddikāru
sentences.l:
They-set-up the-passion in my-heart and-journeyed-off, * and-already have-gone-far with-whom I-love the-dwellings.
Far-off-are from-me the-camping-grounds and-their-dwellers, * and-already is-far the-place-of-visiting, so no place-of-visiting.
And-departed my-endurance from where they-departed, * and-left-me sleep and-patience.
And-since they-journeyed, journeyed-by-night from-me my-joy, * and-already is-lost the-rest, so no rest.
And-they-made-flow with-the-parting (the) tears (of) my-eye, * so-its-tears at-their-separation (are) abundant.
When-ever I-long one-day that I-see-them, * and-grows through-them my-yearning and-waiting,
I-picture their-form in (the) middle (of) my-heart: * passion and-longing and-remembrance.
sentences.i:
They planted passion in my heart and went away, * and the land has carried my beloved far off.
The camps and those who dwelt in them are far from me; * the place of meeting is far, and there is no meeting now.
My fortitude departed when they departed, * and sleep and patience have forsaken me.
Since they set out, my joy has stolen away from me by night; * rest is lost, and there is no rest.
With their parting they set my eye's tears flowing, * and at their going those tears pour down in floods.
Whenever, some day, I long to see them, * and my yearning and my waiting for them grow,
I picture their form within my heart: * all passion, longing and remembrance.
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. The rhyme falls on -āru throughout: al-diyāru / mazāru / iṣṭibāru / qarāru / ghizāru / intiẓāru / iddikāru. The poem plays on its words: bāna … bānū, “departed … they departed”; sārū, “they journeyed”, sarā, “went by night”, and surūrī, “my joy”; and fa-lā mazāru, fa-lā qarāru, “so there is no meeting”, “so there is no rest”, take up the word just used. shaṭṭat bi-man ahwā al-diyāru, “the dwellings have gone far off with the one I love”: bi- marks what they carry off. al-rubūʿ, “camping grounds, abodes”, is printed with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, rabūʿ; wa-sākinīhā, “and their dwellers”, is printed with -ī: either the wa- of accompaniment, which takes the accusative (“together with their dwellers”), or a slip for the nominative sākinūhā, joined to the subject. tajalludī, “my endurance”, is printed with a sukūn on the dāl, where the vowelless mark belongs on the yāʾ. In the fifth line the print points عَيَنِيْ with a fatḥa on the first yāʾ, ʿayanī; the word is ʿaynī, “my eye”, as the metre too requires. فَاَدْمَعُهَا, “and its tears”, is printed with a fatḥa on the mīm, admaʿuhā; admuʿ, a plural of damʿ, “tear”, is meant, and -hā goes back to the eye. bi-baynihimu, “at their parting”: bi- marks the cause, bayn, “separation”; the long -u on the pronoun fills the metre. In the sixth line the print has اَرَاهَمْ, with a fatḥa on the hāʾ, where arāhum, “I see them”, is meant. intiẓār, “waiting”, is printed with a kasra on its alif. iddikār, “remembrance”, is Form VIII of dhakara. The last half-line sets three nouns beside what he pictures: what he holds of them is passion, longing and memory.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَ قَمَرُا لزَّمَانِ يَنْتَظِرُ انْقِضَاءَ الْأَيَّامِ
sentences.tr: thumma jalasa Qamaru al-Zamāni yantaẓiru inqiḍāʾa al-ayyāmi
sentences.l: Then sat Qamar al-Zamān waiting-for (the) passing (of) the-days,
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān sat waiting for the days to pass,
sentences.n: The print sets the name as قمرا لزمان, with the alif of the article slipped onto the first word; it is kept as printed and read Qamaru al-Zamāni. jalasa … yantaẓiru, “he sat waiting”: the imperfect tells what he did as he sat. inqiḍāʾ, Form VII of qaḍā, “coming to an end”; its hamza is printed.

sentences.t: وَحَكَى لِلْخَوْلِيِّ حِكَايَةَ الطُّيُورِ وَمَا وَقَعَ بَيْنَهُمَا فَتَعَجَّبَ الْخَوْلِيُّ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥakā li-al-khawliyyi ḥikāyata al-ṭuyūri wa-mā waqaʿa baynahumā fa-taʿajjaba al-khawliyyu min dhālika
sentences.l: and-he-told to-the-gardener (the) story (of) the-birds and-what happened between-the-two; and-marvelled the-gardener at that.
sentences.i: and he told the gardener the story of the birds and what had passed between the two of them; and the gardener marvelled at it.
sentences.n: ḥakā li-, “to tell to”: li- marks the hearer; ḥikāya, “story”, is from the same root. ṭuyūr, plural of ṭayr, “birds”. baynahumā, “between the two of them”, is dual: the two birds he saw fighting in the tree in Night 212. taʿajjaba min, Form V, “to marvel at”: min marks the cause of wonder; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَامَا إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ فَأَصْبَحَ الْخَوْلِيُّ ضَعِيفًا وَاسْتَمَرَّ عَلَى ضَعْفِهِ يَوْمَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma nāmā ilā al-ṣabāḥi fa-aṣbaḥa al-khawliyyu ḍaʿīfan wa-istamarra ʿalā ḍaʿfihi yawmayni
sentences.l: Then the-two-slept till the-morning; and-was-at-morning the-gardener sick, and-continued in his-sickness two-days;
sentences.i: Then the two of them slept until morning; and in the morning the gardener was sick, and he stayed sick for two days.
sentences.n: nāmā, dual, “the two of them slept”. aṣbaḥa, “to be at morning”, and so “to become”: aṣbaḥa … ḍaʿīfan, “he was sick when morning came”, with the predicate in the accusative. ḍaʿīf, “weak”, in the later language also “ill”, and ḍaʿf, “weakness, illness”. istamarra ʿalā, Form X, “to go on in”: ʿalā marks the state he stays in; its shadda is printed. yawmayni, “for two days”, an accusative of time.

sentences.t: وَفِي ثَالِثِ يَوْمٍ اشْتَدَّ بِهِ الضَّعْفُ حَتَّى يَئِسُوا مِنْ حَيَوٰتِهِ فَحَزِنَ عَلَيْهِ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ حُزْنًا كَثِيرًا
sentences.tr: wa-fī thālithi yawmin ishtadda bihi al-ḍaʿfu ḥattā yaʾisū min ḥayātihi fa-ḥazina ʿalayhi Qamaru al-Zamāni ḥuznan kathīran
sentences.l: and-on (the) third (of a) day grew-hard upon-him the-sickness, until they-despaired of his-life; and-grieved over-him Qamar al-Zamān a-grief great.
sentences.i: and on the third day the sickness grew so heavy upon him that they despaired of his life; and Qamar al-Zamān grieved for him deeply.
sentences.n: thālith yawmin, “the third day”, the ordinal set before its noun in construct. ishtadda bi-, Form VIII, “to grow hard upon”: bi- marks the one it weighs on; its shadda is printed. yaʾisa min, “to despair of”: min marks what is despaired of; the ئ of يئسوا is printed, and “they” are left unnamed. حيوٰته is printed with a dagger alif over the wāw, the old spelling of ḥayāt, “life”, read ḥayātihi. ḥazina ʿalā, “to grieve over”: ʿalā marks the one mourned. ḥuznan kathīran, the verb's own noun as its object, “with great grief”, strengthens the verb.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا هُوَ كَذٰلِكَ وَإِذَا بِالرَّئِيسِ وَالْبَحْرِيَّةُ مَعَهُ قَدْ أَقْبَلُوا وَسَأَلُوا عَنِ الْخَوْلِيِّ
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā huwa ka-dhālika wa-idhā bi-al-raʾīsi wa-al-baḥriyyatu maʿahu qad aqbalū wa-saʾalū ʿani al-khawliyyi
sentences.l: And-while he (was) like-that, and-behold, the-captain, and-the-sailors with-him, had come-up and-asked about the-gardener.
sentences.i: While he was so, behold, the captain came up with the sailors, and they asked after the gardener.
sentences.n: baynamā … wa-idhā, “while … behold”, the turn that brings a sudden arrival: after idhā of surprise, bi- only marks who appears. ka-dhālika, “like that”: ka- compares, “in that state”. al-raʾīs, “the captain” of the ship; its ئ is printed. al-baḥriyya, “the sailors”, a collective; wa-al-baḥriyyatu maʿahu, “the sailors being with him”, is a circumstantial clause. aqbala, Form IV, “to come forward, approach”; the verb is plural for the whole company. saʾala ʿan, “to ask about”: ʿan marks the one asked after; the hamza of وسألوا is printed.

sentences.t: فَأَخْبَرَهُمْ أَنَّهُ ضَعِيفٌ فَقَالُوا أَيْنَ الشَّابُّ الَّذِي يُرِيدُ السَّفَرَ مَعَنَا إِلَى جَزِيرَةِ الْآبَنُوسِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhbarahum annahu ḍaʿīfun fa-qālū ayna al-shābbu alladhī yurīdu al-safara maʿanā ilā jazīrati al-ābanūsi
sentences.l: And-he-told-them that-he (was) sick; and-they-said: Where (is) the-young-man who wants the-journey with-us to (the) island (of) the-ebony?
sentences.i: He told them that he was ill, and they said, “Where is the young man who wants to sail with us to the Isle of Ebony?”
sentences.n: akhbara … anna, “to tell (someone) that”. al-shābb, “the young man”. arāda al-safara, “to want the journey”, with the verbal noun as object. The madda of الآبنوس is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمْ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ هُوَ الْمَمْلُوكُ الَّذِي بَيْنَ أَيْدِيكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahum Qamaru al-Zamāni huwa al-mamlūku alladhī bayna aydīkum
sentences.l: And-said to-them Qamar al-Zamān: He (is) the-slave who (is) between your-hands.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to them, “He is your servant, here before you.”
sentences.n: huwa al-mamlūku alladhī bayna aydīkum, “he is the slave who is between your hands”, a courteous way of saying “here I am, at your service”: mamlūk, “one owned, a slave”, is the humble word for oneself, and bayna aydīkum, “between your hands”, means “before you”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَمَرَهُمْ بِتَحْوِيلِ الْأَمْطَارِ إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ فَنَقَلُوهَا إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ
sentences.tr: thumma amarahum bi-taḥwīli al-amṭāri ilā al-markabi fa-naqalūhā ilā al-markabi
sentences.l: Then he-ordered-them to-(the)-moving (of) the-jars to the-ship, and-they-carried-them to the-ship;
sentences.i: Then he told them to move the jars to the ship, and they carried them aboard.
sentences.n: amara … bi-, “to order (someone) to do”: the verb takes bi- for the thing ordered, here the verbal noun taḥwīl, Form II, “moving, shifting”. al-amṭār, “the jars” of olives and gold. naqala, “to carry over, transfer”.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ أَسْرِعْ فَإِنَّ الرِّيحَ قَدْ طَابَ فَقَالَ لَهُمْ سَمْعًا وَطَاعَةً
sentences.tr: wa-qālū li-Qamari al-Zamāni asriʿ fa-inna al-rīḥa qad ṭāba fa-qāla lahum samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan
sentences.l: and-they-said to-Qamar al-Zamān: Hurry, for indeed the-wind already has-turned-good. And-he-said to-them: Hearing and-obedience.
sentences.i: and they said to Qamar al-Zamān, “Make haste, for the wind is fair.” He answered them with hearing and obedience.
sentences.n: li-Qamari al-Zamāni: li- marks the one spoken to. asriʿ, Form IV imperative, “hurry”. ṭāba, “to be good”, of a wind “to be fair”: the verb is masculine, though rīḥ is usually feminine, as the spoken language often has it. samʿan wa-ṭāʿatan, “hearing and obedience”, accusatives of an unspoken verb (“I give”), the stock reply of one who will do as he is bidden.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَقَلَ زَوَّادَتَهُ إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ وَرَجَعَ إِلَى الْخَوْلِيِّ يُوَدِّعُهُ
sentences.tr: thumma naqala zawwādatahu ilā al-markabi wa-rajaʿa ilā al-khawliyyi yuwaddiʿuhu
sentences.l: Then he-carried his-provisions to the-ship, and-returned to the-gardener bidding-him-farewell.
sentences.i: Then he took his provisions on board, and went back to the gardener to bid him farewell.
sentences.n: zawwāda, “provisions for a journey”, a word of the later language, from zād, “food for the road”. yuwaddiʿuhu, “bidding him farewell”: the imperfect after rajaʿa tells why he went back. waddaʿa, Form II, “to take leave of”; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَهُ فِى النَّزْعِ فَجَلَسَ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ وَغَمَّضَهُ فَفَارَقَتْ رُوحُهُ جَسَدَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadahu fī al-nazʿi fa-jalasa ʿinda raʾsihi wa-ghammaḍahu fa-fāraqat rūḥuhu jasadahu
sentences.l: And-he-found-him in the-death-agony; and-he-sat by his-head and-closed-his-eyes, and-parted his-spirit (from) his-body.
sentences.i: He found him in the throes of death; he sat by his head and closed his eyes, and his spirit left his body.
sentences.n: The print has جسدة, a misprint for جسده, corrected here. nazʿ, “pulling out”, the drawing out of the soul, the death agony; فى is spelt with ى. The hamza of رأسه is printed. ghammaḍa, Form II, “to close the eyes (of someone)”; its shadda is printed. fāraqa, Form III, “to part from, leave”, takes the body as its direct object; rūḥ, “spirit”, is feminine here.

sentences.t: فَجَهَّزَهُ وَوَارَاهُ فِى التُّرَابِ إِلَى رَحْمَةِ اللّٰهِ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-jahhazahu wa-wārāhu fī al-turābi ilā raḥmati Allāhi taʿālā
sentences.l: And-he-made-him-ready and-hid-him in the-earth, (gone) to (the) mercy (of) God, (who is) exalted.
sentences.i: He made him ready for burial and laid him in the earth, gone to the mercy of God Most High.
sentences.n: The print has فجهّزة, a misprint for فجهّزه, and وواراة, a misprint for وواراه, both corrected here. jahhaza, Form II, “to equip”, here to make the dead ready for burial, washed and shrouded; its shadda is printed. wārā, Form III, “to hide, cover”, the decent word for burying: fī marks where, and فى is spelt with ى. ilā raḥmati Allāhi, “to the mercy of God”, is said of the departed. taʿālā, “He is exalted”, the praise that follows God's name.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَوَجَّهَ وَجَاءَ إِلَى الْمَرْكَبِ فَوَجَدَهَا أَرْخَتِ الْقُلُوعَ وَسَارَتْ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تَشُقُّ الْبَحْرَ حَتَّى غَابَتْ عَنْ عَيْنِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma tawajjaha wa-jāʾa ilā al-markabi fa-wajadahā arkhati al-qulūʿa wa-sārat wa-lam tazal tashuqqu al-baḥra ḥattā ghābat ʿan ʿaynihi
sentences.l: Then he-set-out and-came to the-ship, and-he-found-it (had) let-loose the-sails and-gone; and-not it-ceased cleaving the-sea until it-vanished from his-eye.
sentences.i: Then he set out and came to the ship, and found that she had let out her sails and was under way; and she went on cleaving the sea until she was lost to his sight.
sentences.n: The print has تم, a misprint for ثم, corrected here. tawajjaha, Form V, “to set out, turn one's face (towards)”; its shadda is printed. The ship is feminine again: wajadahā, arkhat, sārat. arkhā, Form IV, “to let down, slacken”: arkhati al-qulūʿa, “she let down the sails”, that is, set them to the wind; qulūʿ, plural of qilʿ, “sail”. lam tazal tashuqqu, “she did not cease cleaving”, kept on cutting through; the shadda of تشقّ is printed. ghāba ʿan, “to vanish from”: ʿan marks the one who loses sight.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مَدْهُوشًا حَيْرَانًا لَايَرُدُّ جَوَابًا وَلَا يُبْدِي خِطَابًا
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra Qamaru al-Zamāni madhūshan ḥayrānan lā yaruddu jawāban wa-lā yubdī khiṭāban
sentences.l: And-became Qamar al-Zamān dazed, bewildered, not returning an-answer and-not putting-forth a-speech.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān stood dazed and bewildered, returning no answer and uttering no word.
sentences.n: ṣāra, “to become”, takes its predicate in the accusative. madhūsh, “dazed, stunned”. ḥayrān, “bewildered”, is a diptote in Classical Arabic (ḥayrāna), but the print writes it with the alif of tanwīn, ḥayrānan, as the later language treats it. The print sets lā yaruddu solid as لايردّ, kept so; its shadda is printed. abdā, Form IV, “to show, put forth”. The rhyme falls on jawāban / khiṭāban.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ رَجَعَ إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ فَجَلَسَ مَهْمُومًا مَغْمُومًا يَحْثُو التُّرَابَ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ وَيَلْطِمُ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma rajaʿa ilā al-bustāni fa-jalasa mahmūman maghmūman yaḥthū al-turāba ʿalā raʾsihi wa-yalṭimu ʿalā wajhihi
sentences.l: Then he-returned to the-garden, and-sat anxious, grieved, strewing the-dust upon his-head and-striking upon his-face.
sentences.i: Then he went back to the garden and sat down, careworn and sorrowful, throwing dust upon his head and beating his face.
sentences.n: mahmūm, “anxious, careworn”, and maghmūm, “grieved”, are a rhyming pair. ḥathā, “to throw, strew (dust)”, a sign of mourning, as is laṭama ʿalā wajhihi, “to strike upon one's face”: ʿalā marks where the blows fall. The hamza of رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
